name: Arthrex ACP

lead: Arthrex ACP is a commercial kit that makes platelet-rich plasma (PRP), a concentrate of the patient's own platelets, using a double syringe. Clinics use PRP in sports medicine and in aesthetic medicine for skin, scars and hair.
The appearance link is through PRP's growth factors, which are thought to support tissue healing. Studies of this specific system are small.

paras: A clinician draws a small amount of blood, spins it in the double-syringe device and injects or applies the resulting plasma. Aesthetic uses include facial and scar treatments, sometimes combined with microneedling.
Side effects are generally reported as low. Infection risk arises when equipment is reused: in 2024 the CDC reported HIV infections among patients of an unlicensed spa offering PRP facials.

chain: Blood drawn and concentrated in a double syringe
Growth factors support tissue healing and scar appearance
angle.text: Clinics use ACP plasma to support tissue repair, and one patient survey found higher satisfaction with scars after PRP.[2]

lead: Arthrex ACP (autologous conditioned plasma) is a double-syringe system for preparing platelet-rich plasma from a patient's blood. PRP is a plasma concentrate with platelets at roughly 3 to 5 times normal levels, containing growth factors and cytokines that may stimulate healing.[1]

In aesthetic medicine PRP is injected for wrinkles, fine lines, blemishes and hair loss, and combined 'vampire facials' with microneedling became popular in the 2010s.[1] Preparation varies between clinics and kits, so the products differ.[1][2]

Studies of the Arthrex system include a patient survey on scars after venous access port removal, a five-patient study combining ACP with collagen in tennis elbow, and a comparison of cell and growth factor content across four commercial PRP kits.[3][4][2]

paras: The system separates plasma from whole blood by centrifugation, retaining platelets while removing most red cells.[1] PRP categories vary by leukocyte and fibrin content.[1]

Adverse effects of PRP are generally reported as low.[1] The CDC reported HIV infections in 2024 among patients of an unlicensed spa that reused blood-contaminated equipment during PRP facials.[1] A study of PRP made with NSAIDs present found these medicines affect platelet function in the preparation.[5]

A retrospective survey of 120 patients after venous access port removal compared 100 controls with 20 treated with PRP such as Arthrex ACP; complication rates did not differ, while satisfaction with scarring was higher in the PRP group.[3] In 5 patients with lateral epicondylitis, a single ACP plus collagen injection was followed by reduced pain scores and MRI healing in most cases; the authors called for larger studies.[4] A comparison of four commercial kits in 12 volunteers examined blood cell and growth-factor content.[2]
